findings.quote:
inline fun <reified T : Any> PropertyResolver.getProperty(key: String) : T? =
		getProperty(key, T::class.java)

/**
 * Extension for [PropertyResolver.getProperty] providing a `getProperty<Foo>(...)`
 * variant returning a non-nullable `Foo` with a default value.
 *
 * @author John Burns
 * @since 6.1
 */
inline fun <reified T : Any> PropertyResolver.getProperty(key: String, default: T) : T =
	getProperty(key, T::class.java, default)

/**
 * Extension for [PropertyResolver.getRequiredProperty] providing a
 * `getRequiredProperty<Foo>(...)` variant.
 *
 * @author Sebastien Deleuze
 * @since 5.1
 */
inline fun <reified T: Any> PropertyResolver.getRequiredProperty(key: String) : T =
		getRequiredProperty(key, T::class.java)
findings.explanation: The bracket operator is a separate one-line extension: `resolver[key]` returns `String?` and delegates exactly to the Java member `getProperty(key)`. The three generic extensions are inline and reified with the non-null bound `T : Any`. Nullable lookup returns `T?` and calls `getProperty(key, T::class.java)`; default-valued lookup returns `T` and calls `getProperty(key, T::class.java, default)`; required lookup returns `T` and calls `getRequiredProperty(key, T::class.java)`. Reification supplies the top-level Java runtime `Class`; it does not retain collection-element metadata, so a type such as `List<String>` supplies only the erased `List` class. Kotlin implements none of the source search, fallback, or required-value policy—it only forwards arguments to Java. The non-null declarations for default and required forms do not guarantee successful completion: source, placeholder, or conversion failures can propagate, and required lookup can throw.

Ordinary lookup enters this loop with target `String.class` and nested resolution enabled; typed lookup supplies its requested class and also enables nested resolution; raw-string lookup supplies `String.class` with nested resolution disabled. Sources are visited in collection iteration order, so the first source has highest lookup precedence. A null `PropertySources` collection, an empty collection, or all-null source responses produce null. A null from one source is treated as absent and search continues. The first raw non-null response commits selection to that source: placeholder processing and conversion occur, followed by an immediate return. Consequently, a null conversion result is returned as null without trying lower-priority sources. An exception from the source, placeholder processing, logging hook, or conversion is uncaught and likewise prevents later-source attempts. The resolver has no property-value cache: every lookup reruns iteration and calls source `getProperty` again, although an individual source may have its own behavior.

With nested processing enabled, every source value that is a `String` is resolved before conversion, regardless of requested target type. A non-String `CharSequence` is first converted to text and resolved only when the target is exactly `String.class` or `CharSequence.class`; for targets such as `StringBuilder.class`, nested resolution is skipped. Other value kinds proceed directly to conversion. Empty text bypasses the helper but still reaches the later conversion boundary. Raw lookup disables this source-loop processing, although it still requests conversion to `String`. The placeholder helper deliberately resolves referenced names through `getPropertyAsRawString`, letting the helper control recursive placeholder resolution instead of recursively invoking ordinary nested lookup. Nested lookup is strict by default because `ignoreUnresolvableNestedPlaceholders` starts false; configuring it true selects permissive resolution. Independently, direct `resolvePlaceholders` is always permissive and direct `resolveRequiredPlaceholders` is always strict. They lazily create separate `nonStrictHelper` and `strictHelper` instances. Those helper objects are cached, not resolved property values: each replacement operation invokes the raw-property callback, whose resolver lookup rereads ordered sources.

A null target type returns the original value without consulting any service. With no configured service, an already-assignable value is also returned directly; only a non-assignable value is sent to the shared `DefaultConversionService`. If a service has explicitly been stored, the resolver-level assignability shortcut is bypassed for every non-null target and that service is invoked—even when the value is already assignable. `getConversionService()` uses a volatile field plus synchronized double-checked initialization to create and store an independent `DefaultConversionService`, explicitly distinct from the shared singleton. Merely calling that getter therefore changes later lookups to the configured-service branch and permits modifications to that independent service. `setConversionService` rejects null through `Assert.notNull` (an `IllegalArgumentException`) and stores the supplied service. The conversion result is returned directly and is nullable; null becomes the lookup result. Conversion exceptions are not caught. Nothing at this boundary asserts that every source value is convertible.

The typed default wrapper first performs the complete typed lookup, including source selection, nested-placeholder processing, and conversion; only a final null causes it to return the supplied default. The String default overload follows the same pattern through ordinary String lookup. Defaults themselves are returned directly and are not looked up, placeholder-processed, or converted. Required String and typed lookups likewise run the complete lookup first, then turn a final null into `IllegalStateException`. Thus no source match and a selected source whose configured conversion service returns null have the same wrapper-level outcomes: fallback for default lookup and `IllegalStateException` for required lookup. The selected source is not reconsidered because the source loop already returned the conversion result; these wrappers only inspect that result. By contrast, exceptions from source access, placeholder resolution, or conversion propagate immediately and neither trigger a default nor get replaced by the required-missing exception.
